item.title: California tells Waymo to take the next exit after freeway mishaps (2026)
item.description:
Waymo has suspended driverless freeway rides across the US after California regulators intervened over robotaxis entering construction zones and trying to bypass highway patrol vehicles.

California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide.

The move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned company has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo says freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel.

Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety."

On November 5, three of the company's driverless cars entered an active construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco.

The second incident occurred the following day, and in footage shared widely online, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to drive around highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break – a maneuver used to slow or stop traffic.

"The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," Groveman said in the statement.

Groveman said the DMV had already imposed restrictions and required corrective action following similar incidents on May 18.

Waymo subsequently recalled nearly 4,000 cars after some were caught ignoring road closure signs and cones designating construction zones in Phoenix and San Francisco.

A separate recall covered software affecting nearly 3,800 robotaxis over problems including slowing on high-speed roadways and driving into floodwater.

A Waymo spokesperson said that despite California's temporary ban, its robotaxis continue to operate on city streets across the US.

"Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they said. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state.

"In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week.

"We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations."

Other nuisances and hazards caused by errant Waymos include clogging traffic in thick fog, driving into telephone poles, and killing cats and dogs. ®

item.title: AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites (2026)
item.description:
Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX.

These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services.

“At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register. “We continue to monitor closely and will share updates via myF5 as we learn more.”

As with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years.

Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently.

Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a new reality.”

“We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.” 

NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million), and F5 maintains the open source version.

On Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible.

CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007

Two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.  Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. 

All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5.

“Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld said in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.”

Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8.

Xint found three other NGINX flaws, plus a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel that can be chained with any of the five NGINX vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. The research team dubbed the six bugs “nginx2root.”

The AI-powered offensive security firm also published videos demonstrating attacks using CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the NGINX worker inside a container, and then using the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. These attacks work on AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and bare-metal servers.

AI-powered bug hunting for the win?

"While preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007," the company said in a Wednesday blog. "A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance."

All of these newly-disclosed CVEs point to a larger security issue - especially in light of Tuesday’s Java4Shell, found by AI-bug-hunting-outfit Calif, PHP2Shell (Calif was one of the firms that also used AI to find and weaponize these critical vulns in PHP), and a critical Apache flaw under active exploitation .

“AI is also accelerating vulnerability discovery faster than existing infrastructure was designed to absorb,” Schwartz told us. “Even after a vendor ships a fix, security teams still face heavy manual work in terms of locating vulnerable versions and configurations, testing patches, deploying interim mitigations (such as disabling HTTP/2), and coordinating all of these rollouts.”

There is light at the end of the tunnel, he believes. “In the long run, AI-powered vulnerability research will harden foundational software.”

But in the meantime, it’s a nightmare for security teams, vulnerability managers, and system administrators, who are drowning in the near-daily deluge of CVEs to patch before attackers find and exploit these vulnerabilities.

“Continued collaboration between security researchers, maintainers, and defenders is crucial to absorb the speed and scale of these disclosures,” Schwartz said.®

item.title: Another critical PHP security release has dropped (2026)
item.description: Apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week. The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical.” These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP users to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.” One of the vulnerabilities is another remote code execution (RCE) flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. In October, the PHP Foundation told The Register that it had reserved this CVE identifier for another RCE bug, but added it would not get an emergency fix like the earlier two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities because the third one doesn't pose the same risk. CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register at the time. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.” The earlier informational advisory urged users to “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.” These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled, which the PHP Foundation said is very unlikely in real-world applications. Overall, a large number of bugs were fixed and CVEs patched across five releases. Get more info on the PHP news page here. The November security releases follow a hectic October emergency PHP patch-a-thon, with security teams racing to apply fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell, before attackers could abuse the memory-safety flaws in the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites. While it took miscreants longer to reverse engineer the PHP2Shell fixes than some researchers had anticipated – and the entire internet didn’t burn down in the meantime – the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) did add the two PHP vulns to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26. Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, as early as October 23, according to Dream researchers. The Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said the attackers targeted organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks. ®

item.title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom (2026)
item.description:
Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note.

Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see.

During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not.

"Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door."

Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee.

Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries.

The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically.

The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. 

Contact us

Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

"At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said.

After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in.

The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information. 

"The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®

item.title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts (2026)
item.description: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers. The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise. "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident." TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did. TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected. Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over. Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too. TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems. Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back. "We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said. TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised. Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related. Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®

item.title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions (2026)
item.description: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them. Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. item.title: Russian national accused of stalking San Francisco techie in plot against US defense-tech giant (2026)
item.description:
A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech company in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes.

Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent.

After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed company. 

Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war. 

While unconfirmed officially, the company has widely been reported as Palantir, which did not respond to our request for confirmation.

D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July.

The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the company’s employees.

In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device.

The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims.

D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so. 

One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong. 

D'iu was said to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots. 

The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler.

Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but  claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date.

Inside recruitment

The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations.

According to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 showed that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US.

Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram.

A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to New York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp.

The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically McAllen, Texas - until around that date. Telegram messages would also go on to confirm that he was allegedly helped across the border by an "Uzbek contact" in Mexico.

Records obtained from Google showed D'iu created a Google account in April. According to the affidavit, D'iu used it to search for the company's Wikipedia page on July 28, and on August 3, used Google's AI to devise a route around Texas that bypassed border checkpoints.

The FBI believes D'iu's "spying" began in mid-August, after he bought a laptop, a Wi-Fi device, a puck device, and an additional phone. At this point, the agency claims, he had received his first order to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto company’s office and snap employees' laptop screens before sending copies back to his handlers.

Three days later, D'iu was ordered to go back to a coffee shop and allow his Telegram contacts to remotely control the laptop and collect data from employee devices that were in range, claims the filing.

D'iu was paid $15,000 on three occasions between August 12 and October 6, according to the court documents. To verify the transaction, he was told to send a picture of a dollar bill's serial number to the Telegram contacts, along with a description of what he was wearing. A courier would then arrive, confirming the serial number and handing D'iu the cash.

The filing alleges he used this money to purchase the tech equipment, accommodation, and travel, including a rented silver 2026 Lexus RX 350 from a private owner in Los Angeles on August 22, which he is said to have driven back to San Francisco.

The same Lexus was captured on security footage outside the unnamed company's office on September 1, and over the following two days was implicated in the two instances of female employees being followed. 

Contacted by Palo Alto police on September 4, D'iu confirmed he was the driver who dangerously followed the female staffer for nearly 30 minutes, but claimed he knew nothing about the nearby businesses. D'iu would then claim he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date, and denied following anyone else.

The affidavit goes on to allege that D'iu then traveled to Reno, Nevada, to lay low after his run-in with the police. He spent the time trying to reroute DHL deliveries from San Francisco to his hideout address, which US Customs would later intercept. 

These ended up containing fake IDs with the images the DoJ claims matched D'iu's, including Uzbek documents, a US passport whose number belonged to a New York woman, and a social security card registered to a "Hugo Landry Johns."

He traveled back to the Bay Area in late September, swapping his silver Lexus for a white 2016 Dodge Challenger, and received additional instructions from his handlers, including the order to leave a remote-controlled laptop outside the apartment complex, says the filing.

One Telegram contact named Ian Morales sent photos of at least four employees and their addresses, along with instructions for D'iu to dress as a food delivery worker and visit those locations, asking whoever answered to verify they lived there.

FBI agents executed a search warrant on October 8, seizing a cache of evidence, including what they listed as being:

  • The forged ID documents

  • Two Russian passports

  • $18,035 in cash

  • Two laptops

  • Two iPhones

  • Two T-Mobile SIM cards

  • Wi-Fi equipment

  • A notebook with 10 handwritten addresses supplied by Telegram contacts, along with times the suspect was supposed to attend those locations, at least five of which were for company employees’ homes

  • Profile packages for at least three employees, including: Names, personal information, education and employment histories, names of relatives, narrative histories, and assessments of leadership qualities, strengths, and weaknesses.

Suspicions and charges

Per the affidavit, D'iu was said to have only become suspicious of the tasks he was being ordered to complete in October, when his handlers ordered the laptop to be dropped near the apartment complex.

"D'iu gradually began to understand he was doing something bad and that his actions were illegal," the affidavit stated.

At this point, he allegedly asked the Telegram contacts who he was working for, to which they replied "the Motherland," and the company he was surveilling was involved in providing weapons to Ukraine, resulting in D’iu suspecting the Russian government.

Wong said in the affidavit: "Based on my training, experience, and research, D'iu's communications with his Telegram contacts is consistent with the tactics of [Russian intelligence] and its criminal proxies for spotting, assessing, recruiting, and handling intelligence assets and sources. 

"D'iu's targeting of the company and its employees is also consistent with [Russian intelligence] objectives in Russia's war against Ukraine."

The Russian national was indicted and charged with two counts related to spying offences, and one count related to the fake identity documents. He is next due in court on November 24 but remains in federal custody. ®

item.title: Nvidia adds possible hack to list of very bad things under investigation (2026)
item.description: Finding a new CEO is just one of their problems. Nvidia is investigating an alleged breach following claims by ransomware group The Gentlemen's affiliates that they hacked the AI giant and stole sensitive information. The embattled chipmaker told The Register's that it was investigating a possible third-party data breach. “We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected,” a spokesperson said. “We continue to monitor the situation." The ransomware gang’s data-leak site, shared on social media and seen by The Register, doesn’t show any stolen files or indicate what information the group claims to have stolen. Nvidia first appeared on the criminals’ blog on Wednesday, with The Gentlemen promising “DATA INFO - SOON.” The post also included a countdown, ending November 28. While we can’t verify the criminals’ claims, the group, which emerged in mid-2025, is one of the most prolific ransomware-as-a-service operations. Its affiliates claimed more than 320 victims as of April, with the majority of these alleged ransomware infections (240) occurring in the first half of 2026. The actual count, however, is likely much higher. Check Point researchers accessed an affiliate’s live command-and-control server during an incident response case earlier this year. The server contained victim telemetry that revealed more than 1,570 victims, mostly located in the US, and primarily corporate and organizational environments. According to an operational technology (OT) threat report from Trellix published on Wednesday, industrial ransomware claims jumped nearly 51 percent - to about 1,500 posts- compared to last quarter, and The Gentlemen’s affiliates were the most prolific claim posters during this time period. They accounted for about 16 percent of all posts. In February 2022, an Nvidia data breach exposed employees’ credentials and proprietary code. Extortion crew Lapsus$ claimed to be responsible for that intrusion and data theft.®

item.title: Chase, Visa, Mastercard confirm third-party cyberattacks that may have exposed customers' info (2026)
item.description: JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard have all confirmed that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information after a data-theft-and-extortion gang claimed to have compromised the financial giants. “Visa is aware of these claims,” a spokesperson told The Register on Thursday. “They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week.” Mastercard also cited a third-party provider in an email sent to The Register following our questions about the alleged breach. “We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of a limited amount of email addresses - non-payments information - from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” Mastercard SVP Seth Eisen said. “There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards. At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed.” JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media. “We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack,” America’s largest bank posted on X. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.” According to Chase, the third-party breach didn’t disrupt any of its services, and it’s not connected to the outages earlier in the week attributed to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems. “There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” the bank said on Thursday. None of the three financial firms would comment on who the third-party providers are, when the breaches occurred, and what specific data was stolen. The Register will update this story as we learn more details about the intrusions. Extortion crew n0n claimed responsibility for all three alleged hacks, posting the financial giants to its data-leak site on Monday. The group, believed to be based in Russia, emerged in September and posted 108 victims over its first month in operations. ®

item.title: Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way (2026)
item.description: The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023. "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them." Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime. "At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption." Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering. Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained. Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network. "Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life." At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play. Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content." Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements. "I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device." If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success. But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky. Bluesky launched Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. item.title: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else (2026)
item.description: If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories. VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite. VMware also wants its users to address CVE-2026-123891, which allows attackers to read and write the database used by SDDC Manager, the tool for managing entire software-defined datacenters. Attackers can execute arbitrary commands and elevate privileges to root. The prospect of an unknown party getting access to vCenter or SDDC manager is not pleasant. At least VMware has fixed its software. The virty giant hasn't done the same to address a second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, which warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618). VMware plans to ship new versions of its products with a patched version of Apache, but for now only has workarounds that disable the http2 protocol. A KVM curiosity Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours. This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host. It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses. This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5. Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Terra Security says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs. Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18. Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours. The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment. Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE. The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®

item.title: Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in (2026)
item.description: A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2. The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again." Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored." Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID. Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected. An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets. Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

item.title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand (2026)
item.description: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government. The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters. The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month. A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers. For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected. While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand. At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens. In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US. Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators. Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless. Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not. What the judgment does not confirm While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public. "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest. "We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed. "That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now." The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026. The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users. The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals. A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public. "A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data. "Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so. "Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies." Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

item.title: Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses (2026)
item.description: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities. The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor. In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call. Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events. The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role." A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense. "Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. "AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified." The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary. The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI. The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured. On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera. Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.” Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim. "As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said. The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders." Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy. "It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said. "Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience." Smart specs can't shake the hate When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees. "Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time. Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces. Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time. Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas. On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones. However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning. With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general. A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children. There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy. A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament. The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

item.title: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server (2026)
item.description: Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses. The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance. In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory. On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register. The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time. Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools. Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents. "Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote. Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server. "The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server." Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root. In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code. Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies. This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies. "Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

item.title: Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy (2026)
item.description: Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal President Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3, currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers. First the flood, then the dams While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome. AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants. Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others. Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few. The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy. Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ® Correction: An earlier version of this article misstated Meredith Whitaker's title. She is the president of the Signal Foundation.

item.title: Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers (2026)
item.description: Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses. On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information. Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand. Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers. “We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.” Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program. According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said. It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker. Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text, and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26. “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.” Customer data has left the building The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published. All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra. In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker said, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.” Qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®

item.title: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here (2026)
item.description: On Thursday, PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month. For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances. The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation, responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep. In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings. Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults. Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.” No cookies for impostors In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline. Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit. For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote. Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before. Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote. Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link. Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry. The new release brings some other security-minded changes as well. The PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight. Continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs. Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of new goodies. PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability. The new edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range. Another tricky day for PHP devs For administrators, this PHP update round may be a bit of a shambles. As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post, these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves. “In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the new default,” he wrote. Despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability. ®
